claim: Did you know… countries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel Prizes?

studies.cite: Messerli (2012), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: Plotted national chocolate consumption against Nobel laureates per capita and reported a strong positive correlation across countries.
studies.verdict: Country-level correlation; wealth and research funding explain it, not cocoa.

claim: Did you know… coffee drinking was once linked to a doubled risk of pancreatic cancer?

studies.cite: MacMahon et al. (1981), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In a hospital case-control study, drinking three or more cups daily carried a relative risk of 2.7 for pancreatic cancer.
studies.verdict: Control group included many patients with digestive disorders; the finding did not hold.

studies.cite: Turati et al. (2012), Annals of Oncology
studies.finding: A meta-analysis of coffee and pancreatic cancer found no appreciable association, including at high consumption.
studies.verdict: Meta-analysis: coffee is not appreciably related to pancreatic cancer risk.

claim: Did you know… taking vitamin E supplements cut women's heart disease risk by a third?

studies.cite: Stampfer et al. (1993), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: Among 87,245 nurses, those with the highest vitamin E intake had roughly one-third lower coronary risk, mostly from supplements.
studies.verdict: Observational; the authors themselves urged waiting for randomized trials.

studies.finding: In 11,324 heart-attack survivors, vitamin E did not reduce death, nonfatal heart attack, or stroke.
studies.verdict: Randomized trial: no benefit from vitamin E.

studies.cite: Yusuf et al. (2000), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In 9,541 high-risk patients, 400 IU of vitamin E daily for five years did not reduce cardiovascular events.
studies.verdict: Randomized trial: no cardiovascular benefit over five years.

claim: Did you know… a compound in red wine helps mice live longer?

studies.finding: Middle-aged mice on a high-calorie diet given resveratrol survived longer and had improved insulin sensitivity and motor function.
studies.verdict: Real in mice on a rich diet; human benefit not shown.

studies.cite: Semba et al. (2014), JAMA Internal Medicine
studies.finding: In 783 older Italians, urinary resveratrol metabolites were not associated with lower mortality, heart disease, or cancer.
studies.verdict: Observational human data show no link; supplement trials remain mixed.

claim: Did you know… eating breakfast is linked to a healthier weight?

studies.cite: Dhurandhar et al. (2014), American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
studies.finding: In 309 overweight adults, 16 weeks of eating or skipping breakfast produced no significant difference in weight loss.
studies.verdict: Randomized trial: no effect on weight.

studies.finding: A meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials found breakfast eaters did not lose more weight; skippers weighed 0.44 kg less.
studies.verdict: Observational link likely reflects confounding by lifestyle and socioeconomic status.

claim: Did you know… sitting for long periods raises the risk of early death?

studies.cite: Biswas et al. (2015), Annals of Internal Medicine
studies.finding: A review of 47 studies linked more sedentary time to higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.24), even among active people.
studies.verdict: Observational; sitting and physical activity were measured inconsistently.

studies.finding: Pooled data on over one million people suggested 60 to 75 minutes of daily moderate activity offsets mortality risk from sitting.
studies.verdict: Contested: risk attenuated by exercise, though high television time remained linked.

claim: Did you know… coffee drinkers die less often, even from accidents?

studies.cite: Freedman et al. (2012), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: Among about 400,000 older adults, those drinking three or more cups daily had roughly 10 percent lower mortality than non-drinkers.
studies.verdict: Association persists in cohorts; lower accident deaths point to confounding.

claim: Did you know… every half egg per day was tied to higher mortality?

studies.finding: Across six US cohorts of 29,615 adults, each extra half egg daily was associated with higher cardiovascular disease and mortality risk.
studies.verdict: Egg link vanished after adjusting for dietary cholesterol; debate unresolved.

claim: Did you know… a Mediterranean diet study was retracted and republished, and still held?

studies.cite: Estruch et al. (2013), New England Journal of Medicine (retracted 2018)
studies.finding: A randomized trial reported about 30 percent fewer cardiovascular events with a Mediterranean diet plus olive oil or nuts.
studies.verdict: Retracted for randomization irregularities at some sites; not fraud.

studies.cite: Estruch et al. (2018), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: Reanalysis, excluding 1,588 participants with possible randomization departures and adjusting for clustering, reached largely the same conclusion.
studies.verdict: Republished; the Mediterranean diet effect largely stood.
